analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare HMOs to pay for emergency care without prior approval, even at out-of-network hospitals.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by nine senators from both parties, never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare beneficiaries enrolled in HMOs could be stuck paying for emergency room visits when the plan refused to authorize care or when the hospital was outside the plan's network. This bill would have required Medicare HMOs to cover emergency services using a 'prudent layperson' standard — if a reasonable person would think it was an emergency — without prior approval, with no penalty for using an out-of-network hospital, and with no higher copay than in-network care. It would also have required HMOs to staff a 24-hour authorization line and treat care as approved if no one answered within 30 minutes.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries enrolled in managed care plans, who would no longer risk bearing the full cost of an emergency room visit because their HMO denied authorization, refused to pay an out-of-network hospital, or charged higher coinsurance for emergency care.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare risk-contract HMOs would have to cover emergency services regardless of whether the treating hospital had a contract with the plan, and without requiring prior authorization [S3].

Plans could not impose cost-sharing on emergency department care calculated more harshly than for comparable services in other settings, though a reasonable flat copay to deter inappropriate use would still be allowed [S3].

The bill defines an emergency medical condition using the 'prudent layperson' standard — whether a typical person with average knowledge of health could expect serious jeopardy without immediate care — rather than leaving the judgment to the plan [S3].

Plans would have to provide 24/7 access to someone authorized to approve urgently needed care identified during emergency screening, and care would be deemed approved if no one responded within 30 minutes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare risk-contract HMOs, which would have to pay out-of-network emergency providers promptly and absorb more emergency claims; some of that cost could show up in plan premiums or reduced extras.

drawbacks.text: The bill allows plans to impose a 'reasonable copayment' set by the Secretary to deter inappropriate emergency department use, so beneficiaries would still owe something per visit [S3].

Covering out-of-network emergency care and 24/7 authorization adds cost to plans; a fair objection is that plans could recoup it through higher premiums or leaner supplemental benefits, spreading the cost to all enrollees [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection is straightforward and aimed at a real harm: people who believed they were having an emergency should not be financially punished because their HMO later decided it was not one, or because the nearest hospital was out of network. The costs to plans are real but modest relative to the risk shifted onto sick seniors, and the bill keeps a copay tool to discourage non-emergency use. The main weakness is procedural — it was introduced in late September of an election year with weeks left in the session, giving it essentially no path to passage.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Graham introduced the bill on September 25, 1996, with senators from both parties including Grassley, Chafee, Jeffords, Baucus, Moseley-Braun, Simon, Hollings, and Wellstone [S3].
Eight senators cosponsored, three Republicans and five Democrats [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; the committee took no further action, and the Congress ended January 3, 1997 with no vote ever taken [S5].
The bill's entire recorded action history is introduction, introductory remarks, and committee referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare HMOs benefited from the bill's death: they avoided a federal requirement to pay promptly for out-of-network emergency care without prior authorization. Seniors in those plans kept bearing the risk of denied or underpaid emergency claims.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare HMOs, which avoided new payment duties

for.name: Sen. Bob Graham
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it with remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 8 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Finance Committee members Chuck Grassley and Max Baucus.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start: a Democrat from Florida led a group that included three Republicans and five Democrats as cosponsors [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have forced plans covering emergency services to pay for emergency care without prior authorization, cover out-of-network hospitals, and cap emergency cost-sharing. Their interest in avoiding those payment obligations ran directly against beneficiaries' financial protection in emergencies.
